'Treacherous' and the 12 m waves are the page's own statements ('is considered one of the most treacherous voyages', 'waves top 40 feet (12 m)') and are said as the page says them; the page calls the Antarctic Circumpolar Current 'the strongest oceanic current' with an estimated 100 to 150 Sv. Not used: the page's three definitions of the Atlantic-Pacific boundary (it names more than one), the date range for when the passage opened (49 to 17 million years ago, a debate), and the oceanography detail. The two map markers are the coordinates the Cape Horn and Livingston Island pages give. No maritime limits and no Antarctic territory are drawn or named; Chile and Argentina both appear only as land, unlabelled.

claims.text: The Drake Passage is the body of water between Cape Horn in Chile at the southern extreme of the South American mainland and the South Shetland Islands of Antarctica; it connects the southwestern part of the Atlantic Ocean (Scotia Sea) with the southeastern part of the Pacific Ocean.
Traversing the Drake Passage is considered one of the most treacherous voyages for ships to make.

The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, which runs through it, meets no resistance from any landmass, and waves top 40 feet (12 m), giving it a reputation for being 'the most powerful convergence of seas'.
The 800-kilometre-wide passage between Cape Horn and Livingston Island is the shortest crossing from Antarctica to another landmass.
The Drake Passage is the narrowest passage (choke point) around Antarctica.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the strongest oceanic current, has an estimated transport of 100 to 150 Sv (Sverdrups, million cubic metres per second) through the passage.
On December 25, 2019, a crew of six explorers successfully rowed across the passage, becoming the first in history to do so.
In 1616, Dutch navigator Willem Schouten became the first to sail around Cape Horn and through the Drake Passage.
The passage received its English name from Sir Francis Drake, who was blown far south in a tempest in 1578 after passing through the Strait of Magellan.

The Strait of Magellan and the Beagle Channel have frequent narrows, little room to manoeuvre, and unpredictable winds and tidal currents, so most sailing ships prefer the Drake Passage, which is open water for hundreds of miles.
